topics.title: Device Vulnerabilities and Attacks
topics.hook: A smart thermostat on a company network hasn't been updated in three years and still has the password 'admin'. Why would an attacker start there instead of the CEO's laptop?
concept: Devices range from servers and personal computers to handhelds (phones, tablets), embedded systems (controllers inside machines), and IoT devices (cameras, sensors, smart appliances). IoT and embedded devices are often the weakest: default passwords, rare updates, little monitoring.

Common device vulnerabilities: unpatched software, default or weak credentials, unnecessary open ports and services (Telnet on port 23 sends passwords in cleartext), autorun of removable media, and missing BIOS/UEFI passwords that let someone change boot settings.

Malware types: a virus attaches to files and needs a user to run it; a worm self-replicates across networks; a trojan disguises itself as legitimate software; a RAT (remote access trojan) gives remote control; ransomware encrypts data for payment; spyware and keyloggers record activity; a logic bomb triggers on a condition or date; a rootkit hides deep in the system to keep privileged access; fileless malware runs in memory using built-in tools, leaving little on disk.
terms: Internet-connected everyday device such as a camera or sensor.
Computer built into a larger machine with a dedicated function.
Self-replicating malware that spreads without user action.
Remote access trojan granting an attacker remote control.
Malware that encrypts data and demands payment.
Records keystrokes to capture passwords and data.
Malicious code triggered by a specific condition or time.
Malware hiding its presence while keeping privileged access.
Runs in memory using legitimate system tools, leaving few files.

compare.title: Virus vs. worm vs. trojan
rows: Attaches to files; needs a user to run it
User installs it believing it's legitimate

traps: A worm needs no user action; a virus does.
Fileless malware is hard for traditional antivirus because there's little file to scan.

items.stem: Malware spreads from computer to computer across a network with no user clicking anything. It is MOST likely a:
items.why: Self-propagation without user action defines a worm.

items.stem: A free 'PDF converter' app secretly opens a backdoor for an attacker to control the PC. This is BEST described as a:
items.why: Disguised software providing remote control is a RAT.

items.stem: Why are IoT devices frequent attack targets?
opts: They often ship with default credentials and are rarely updated
They are always behind a DMZ
items.why: Weak defaults and poor patching make IoT easy footholds.

items.stem: Code planted by a disgruntled admin deletes payroll files if his account is ever disabled. This is a:
items.why: Malicious code triggered by a condition is a logic bomb.

items.stem: Files on a shared drive are suddenly unreadable and a note demands cryptocurrency. Which malware is this?
items.why: Encrypting data for payment is ransomware.

items.stem: Antivirus scans find nothing, but suspicious PowerShell commands run in memory at each login. Which type is MOST likely?
opts: Boot sector virus on a floppy
items.why: In-memory execution via built-in tools is characteristic of fileless malware.

items.stem: A server has Telnet (port 23) open to the network. Why is this a significant risk?
opts: Telnet sends credentials in cleartext that can be sniffed
items.why: Unencrypted remote login exposes passwords.

items.stem: An audit finds lab PCs automatically run programs from any inserted USB drive. How should this risk be documented?
opts: Autorun enabled: removable media can execute malware without user intent
items.why: Autorun is a device vulnerability enabling malware execution.

topics.title: Authentication
topics.hook: A website was breached and its password file leaked. One site stored passwords as SHA-256 hashes with unique salts; another stored them as plain MD5. Which users should panic?
concept: Systems should never store passwords in plaintext. They store a cryptographic hash: a one-way function that turns input into a fixed-length digest. Good hashes have pre-image resistance (you can't reverse the digest) and collision resistance (it's hard to find two inputs with the same digest). MD5 and SHA-1 are deprecated; SHA-256 and SHA-512 are current. Windows uses NTHash.
A salt is a random value added to each password before hashing, so identical passwords produce different hashes and precomputed rainbow tables become useless.

Password attacks: brute force tries every combination; a dictionary attack tries likely words; a rainbow table looks up precomputed hashes; password spraying tries a few common passwords across many accounts (dodging lockouts); credential stuffing reuses leaked username/password pairs. Defenses include MFA (factors: knowledge, possession, inherence/biometric, location), and login policies: minimum length, complexity, maximum age, password history, and account lockout after repeated failures.
terms: One-way function producing a fixed-length digest.
Random value added before hashing to make each hash unique.
Infeasible to recover input from its hash.
Two different inputs producing the same hash.
Precomputed table of hashes for common passwords.
Few common passwords tried against many accounts.
Using leaked credential pairs on other sites.
Disabling login after a set number of failures.
traps: Hashing is not encryption: there's no key to decrypt a hash.
Account lockout stops online guessing but does nothing against offline cracking of a stolen hash file.

items.stem: Why are passwords stored as hashes rather than plaintext?
opts: If the database leaks, the original passwords aren't directly revealed
Hashes can be decrypted by users
items.why: A one-way hash protects passwords even if the stored data is stolen.

items.stem: What does adding a unique salt to each password before hashing MOST directly defeat?
items.why: Salts make precomputed hash tables useless.

items.stem: Logs show the password 'Spring2027!' tried once against 3,000 different accounts. Which attack is this?
items.why: One common password across many accounts is spraying.

items.stem: Which pair represents two DIFFERENT authentication factors?
items.why: Biometric (inherence) plus knowledge are different factor types.

items.stem: Which hash algorithm should be AVOIDED for new password storage?
items.why: MD5 is deprecated due to weaknesses.

items.stem: An admin configures: lockout after 5 failed attempts for 15 minutes. Which attack does this MOST effectively slow?
opts: Online brute force against a single account
Offline cracking of a stolen hash file
Password spraying with one attempt per account
items.why: Lockout limits guesses per account online; offline cracking and low-rate spraying avoid it.

items.stem: Two users both chose 'sunshine1'. On a system WITHOUT salting, what can an attacker who steals the hash file conclude?
opts: Both users have the same password, because their hashes match
items.why: Unsalted identical passwords produce identical hashes.

items.stem: A policy says users may not reuse any of their last 10 passwords. Which setting is this?
items.why: Remembering past passwords to block reuse is password history.

topics.title: Protecting Devices
topics.hook: A laptop's antivirus definitions are 9 months old, it hasn't installed an update since summer, and its firewall allows all outbound traffic. Fix it in three moves.
concept: Managerial controls for devices: an acceptable use policy (what users may do), a password policy, and a software installation policy (only approved apps, ideally installed by IT). These reduce risk before any tool runs.

Anti-malware software scans files and behavior, matching signatures of known malware, and quarantines suspicious files (isolating them so they can't run but can still be examined). It needs regular signature updates.

Patching fixes known vulnerabilities; attackers often exploit flaws for which patches already exist. A host-based firewall runs on the device itself with its own ACL, filtering inbound and outbound traffic. Outbound rules can block data exfiltration channels, for example blocking outbound FTP from a workstation that has no reason to use it.
terms: Rules for appropriate use of organizational systems.
Limits which applications may be installed and by whom.
Isolating a suspicious file so it can't execute.
Update that fixes bugs or security vulnerabilities.
Firewall running on an individual device.
Restricting traffic leaving a device or network.

compare.title: Network vs. host firewall
rows: Can't see traffic inside a segment

traps: Quarantine is not deletion. The file is isolated and kept for analysis.
A network firewall doesn't protect a laptop on hotel Wi-Fi; a host firewall still does.

items.stem: Why do software updates improve security?
opts: They patch known vulnerabilities attackers could exploit
items.why: Patches close publicly known holes.

items.stem: Anti-malware moves a suspicious file to an isolated area where it can't run. This action is:
items.why: Isolating a file so it can't execute is quarantine.

items.stem: To stop a compromised workstation from sending files out over FTP, which host firewall rule is BEST?
items.why: Blocking outbound FTP (port 21) cuts that exfiltration channel.

items.stem: A document listing what employees may and may not do with company laptops is a:
items.why: An AUP defines appropriate use.

items.stem: Signature-based anti-malware is LEAST effective against:
opts: New malware with no known signature
items.why: Signatures only match known patterns.

items.stem: Which combination BEST protects a laptop that travels between offices and hotels?
opts: Host-based firewall, current patches, updated anti-malware, and VPN
items.why: Endpoint controls go wherever the device goes.

items.stem: Only IT may install software on school devices. This is which control?
items.why: Restricting installs is a managerial software policy.

items.stem: A patch for a critical, actively exploited vulnerability was released 2 months ago but not installed. How should the risk be rated?
opts: Zero risk because a patch exists
Low impact because it's a laptop
items.why: Known, exploited, and unpatched means high likelihood and severe impact.

topics.title: Detecting Attacks on Devices
topics.hook: An auth log shows 400 failed logins in 90 seconds from one IP, each against a different username, then one success. What attack, and what do you do first?
concept: Device detection relies on logs and indicators. Authentication logs record login attempts with time, user, source IP, and result. User activity logs, access logs, and system configuration files reveal what happened after login.

Indicators of compromise come in three kinds: host-based (new admin accounts, disabled security tools, changed settings), file-based (unexpected or modified files, known-bad hashes), and behavior-based (unusual processes, logins at odd hours, data transfers). Endpoint detection and response (EDR) tools monitor these continuously and can isolate a device. Hybrid detection combines signatures and behavior.

Reading auth logs: many failures against one account suggests brute force; one or two attempts across many accounts from one IP in seconds suggests spraying; successful logins from unusual locations or times suggest stolen credentials. Offline attacks on a stolen hash file can't be detected in logs at all, since no login attempt reaches the system. Detection also has a cost: heavy monitoring can slow devices.
terms: Record of login attempts: user, time, source, success or failure.
Evidence on a device, such as new accounts or altered settings.
Suspicious or modified files, or known-malicious hashes.
Abnormal actions such as odd-hour logins or unusual processes.
Endpoint detection and response: monitors endpoints, alerts, and can isolate.
Cracking stolen hashes without contacting the system; leaves no logs.

compare.title: Auth log patterns
rows: One try each, many users, one IP, seconds apart
Success from new country at 3 a.m.
No failed attempts but account taken over

traps: No failed logins doesn't mean no attack. Offline cracking and phishing leave none.
EDR is detective and responsive; it complements, not replaces, patching.

items.stem: An auth log shows 250 failed logins for user 'jsmith' in 3 minutes from one IP. Which attack is MOST likely?
items.why: Many attempts against one account indicate brute force.

items.stem: Logs show one failed login each for 800 different users from the same IP within 60 seconds. Which attack is this?
items.why: Few attempts per account, many accounts, one source is spraying.

items.stem: Why can't authentication logs detect an attacker cracking a stolen password-hash file?
opts: The cracking happens offline, so no login attempts reach the system
items.why: Offline attacks never touch the live login system.

items.stem: A new local administrator account appears on a server that no one created. This is BEST classified as a:
items.why: Unauthorized system changes on a host are host-based indicators.

items.stem: Which tool continuously monitors endpoints for suspicious behavior and can isolate an infected device?
items.why: EDR provides endpoint monitoring and response.

items.stem: A user's account logs in successfully at 03:12 from another country, with no prior failures. The user was asleep. What is MOST likely?
opts: Credentials were stolen (e.g., phishing or reuse) and used directly
items.why: A clean success at an abnormal time and place suggests stolen credentials.

items.stem: A school enables full real-time scanning of every file on old laptops and students complain of lag. What tradeoff is this?
items.why: Heavier monitoring consumes resources.

items.stem: Which detection approach BEST catches both known malware and suspicious new behavior?
items.why: Hybrid combines the strengths of both.
